summary: Apple ARKit and RealityKit are the sensing half and the simulation-and-drawing half of one closed device platform: ARKit reads the room, the hands and the world position, RealityKit holds the entity-component scene, runs the physics and audio, and draws the frame in Metal. Scored together they cover more of this map than any other single subject in the geospatial and input rows: location anchors placed by latitude and longitude, visual positioning that matches the camera image against Apple's own street imagery, shared and persistent anchors on both device families, articulated hand tracking, and — new and easy to miss — a first-party Gaussian splat renderer. Interchange runs entirely through OpenUSD, which is the platform's real strength: USD references and overrides give genuine non-destructive composition, and USDKit now exposes layers and stages to Swift. Four traps a standards reader should carry away. First, the platform reads USD far better than it honours it: RealityKit ignores every light authored in a USD file, its MaterialX support is documented as lossy, and physics data does not load through USDKit at all. Second, the interactive parts of the format — anchoring, behaviours, three-dimensional text — are Apple's own preliminary schemas, which Apple itself warns can change at any time. Third, on Apple Vision Pro the app is never told where the person is looking, by design, so any standard that assumes app-readable gaze will not compose here. Fourth, everything shared is same-app and near-field: synchronisation runs over peer-to-peer Multipeer Connectivity or a FaceTime-backed SharePlay session, there is no world address, no handoff between publishers, and no interest management or prediction.

coverage.note: RealityKit draws the scene itself and is the renderer Apple's own apps and system viewers use for USD content; the pass structure is not exposed, and the only developer hook into the frame is a post-process callback.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: RealityKit
sources.quote: RealityKit provides high-performance 3D simulation and rendering capabilities you can use to create apps with 3D or augmented reality (AR) for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, and visionOS.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
sources.quote: Depending on the device, its operating system, and the app, there are four renderers that might display your 3D assets: RealityKit, Raytracer, Storm, or SceneKit.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: RealityRenderer
sources.quote: A renderer that displays a RealityKit scene in an existing Metal workflow.

coverage.note: The renderer targets Metal only. Custom shading is written in Metal, and a RealityKit scene can be driven inside an existing Metal workflow; there is no path to any other graphics interface.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: RealityRenderer
sources.quote: A renderer that displays a RealityKit scene in an existing Metal workflow.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: CustomMaterial
sources.quote: Custom, or programmable, materials allow you to leverage RealityKit’s existing shader pipeline to render physically based or unlit materials that support custom Metal shader functions.

coverage.note: Three material kinds ship: a physically based material that mirrors what USDZ carries, a shader-graph material built in Reality Composer Pro or loaded from MaterialX, and a custom material with Metal surface shaders and geometry modifiers.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicallyBasedMaterial
sources.quote: A Physically Based Rendering (PBR) material is a material that closely approximates the way light reflects off of real-world objects.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ShaderGraphMaterial
sources.quote: A material that comes from a shader graph in a Reality Composer Pro project, or a MaterialX shader.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: CustomMaterial
sources.quote: Custom, or programmable, materials allow you to leverage RealityKit’s existing shader pipeline to render physically based or unlit materials that support custom Metal shader functions.

coverage.note: Image-based lighting, directional, point and spot lights, baked lightmaps and diffuse probes are all in the framework. The trap for interchange: RealityKit ignores every light authored inside a USD file and lights the scene from the real room instead, so a lighting rig does not survive the move into this renderer.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: EnvironmentResource
sources.quote: RealityKit supports image-based lighting that enables realistic reflections on your scene’s 3D content.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Global illumination and baked lighting
sources.quote: Light scenes realistically by precomputing illumination so surfaces pick up bounced color and ambient detail without recalculating it every frame.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
sources.quote: Because RealityKit is an AR-first renderer, it doesn’t use any lights included in a USD file, and instead bases its lighting on the scene’s real-world lighting.

coverage.note: A registered callback receives the finished frame before display, and bloom and tone mapping ship as components.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Postprocessing effects
sources.quote: In iOS 15 and later, and macOS 12 and later, you can apply postprocess effects to a RealityKit scene after RealityKit renders it, but before RealityKit displays it.

coverage.note: There is no level-of-detail or streaming-order mechanism in either framework. Apple's own guidance is to do it by hand at authoring time: size each asset for how large it will appear and cut big meshes into pieces so off-camera parts can be culled.

sources.quote: Split large geometry into chunks.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: Scale detail to viewer distance.

coverage.note: RealityKit renders three-dimensional Gaussian splats through a dedicated component, with spherical-harmonic colour, sorting and projection modes. It reads no splat file: the app parses PLY, USD or any other container itself and fills GPU buffers, so there is no interchange path, only a rendering path.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: GaussianSplatComponent
sources.quote: Use a Gaussian splat component to display volumetric imagery captured from real environments, coalesced into 3D Gaussian splats (3DGS).

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: GaussianSplatComponent
sources.quote: The framework doesn’t load files directly, so you parse your source format — PLY, USD, or any other container — and populate the buffers yourself.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: GaussianSplatComponent
sources.quote: Scene lighting doesn’t affect a Gaussian splat asset.

coverage.note: Captured scenes reach the screen as splats, and stereoscopic and Apple Immersive Video play through a video component; a point cloud is drawn only inside the object-capture scanning view. There is no general voxel or point-cloud renderer and no volumetric video codec in the frameworks themselves.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: GaussianSplatComponent
sources.quote: Use a Gaussian splat component to display volumetric imagery captured from real environments, coalesced into 3D Gaussian splats (3DGS).

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Immersive Media Support
sources.quote: Immersive Media Support enables you to create custom workflows for processing Apple Immersive Video (AIV).

coverage.note: Text becomes an extruded mesh through a generator on the mesh resource, and USD assets can carry text through Apple's preliminary text schema.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MeshResource.generateText
sources.quote: Generates a 3D mesh for rendering static text.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: OpenUSD schemas for AR
sources.quote: Annotate the environment by displaying text.

coverage.note: In an AR session the device camera is the viewpoint; outside one, a perspective camera entity sets it, and RealityRenderer takes an explicit active camera.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PerspectiveCamera
sources.quote: During an AR session, RealityKit automatically uses the device’s camera to define the perspective from which to render the scene.

coverage.note: The scene is an entity tree with components attached; Reality Composer Pro authors the same entity-component-system model that the runtime executes.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Entity
sources.quote: An element of a RealityKit scene to which you attach components that provide appearance and behavior characteristics for the entity.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Reality Composer Pro
sources.quote: Reality Composer Pro is a 3D content creation platform backed by an Entity Component System (ECS).

coverage.note: Every entity carries a transform of scale, rotation as a unit quaternion, and translation. The frame is Y-up and right-handed, which matches OpenUSD and glTF and differs from the left-handed engines.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Transform
sources.quote: A component that defines the scale, rotation, and translation of an entity.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: RealityKit uses Y-up orientation and meters as its unit scale.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ARFaceAnchor
sources.quote: The coordinate system is right-handed—the positive x direction points to the viewer’s right (that is, the face’s own left), the positive y direction points up (relative to the face itself, not to the world), and the positive z direction points outward from the face (toward the viewer).

coverage.note: The container is OpenUSD: the loader reads .usd, .usda, .usdc, .usdz and Apple's own .reality file. RealityKit itself only loads; authoring USD is USDKit's job, and Object Capture and RoomPlan are the parts of the platform that write it.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Loading entities from a file
sources.quote: You can load USD files (.usd, .usda, .usdc, .usdz) and Reality files (.reality) this way.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: USD
sources.quote: USD is also Apple’s format of choice for 3D Content, including 3D content used for Augmented Reality.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: USDKit
sources.quote: USDKit is the Swift API for authoring, composing, and manipulating Universal Scene Description (USD) content.

coverage.note: Geometry arrives as USD meshes, in text or binary form; procedural primitives, extruded paths and a low-level mesh with an app-defined vertex layout are all available at runtime.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: USDC is a binary format. It is more compact and faster to load than USDA, making it the preferred format for geometry-heavy assets and large scenes.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MeshResource
sources.quote: A high-level representation of a collection of vertices and edges that define a shape.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: LowLevelMesh
sources.quote: A container for vertex data that you can use to create and update meshes using your own format.

coverage.note: Textures load into GPU-resident resources with optional ASTC compression, and the USDZ archive is limited to four image encodings.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: TextureResource
sources.quote: A texture resource holds pixel data accessible by the GPU, organized as an image, a cube of images, an array of images, or a 3D image (volume texture).

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: TextureResource.Compression
sources.quote: Compression allows varying levels of memory usage gains at the cost of image-quality reduction.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: USD files may use a wide range of texture formats, however USDZ files may only include JPEG, PNG, EXR, and AVIF.

coverage.note: MaterialX comes in, but not without loss. A shader-graph material can be built straight from MaterialX data, and Apple publishes the exact places RealityKit falls short of the specification: one packed texture per material, two UV sets, and only the first texture transform in a material is honoured.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ShaderGraphMaterial
sources.quote: A material that comes from a shader graph in a Reality Composer Pro project, or a MaterialX shader.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
sources.quote: RealityKit supports only a single packed texture per material.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
sources.quote: RealityKit supports two UV Sets.

coverage.note: Animation resources travel inside the asset file and are played, sequenced, grouped and looped at runtime; Reality Composer Pro adds multi-track sequences and an animation graph.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: AnimationResource
sources.quote: Animation resources come bundled with an entity when you load the entity from a file.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Reality Composer Pro
sources.quote: Reality Composer Pro includes editors and workflows for designing materials with Shader Graph, building visual scripts with Script Graph, authoring GPU-driven simulations with Compute Graph, defining character behaviors with Animation Graphs, and editing skeletons.

coverage.note: A mesh carries a joint hierarchy and per-vertex joint influences, and the runtime exposes named skeletal poses for reading and writing. One constraint on the way in: Apple asks authors to merge several rigs into a single joint hierarchy before export.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MeshResource.Skeleton
sources.quote: A skeleton consists of a hierarchy of joints.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SkeletalPosesComponent
sources.quote: A component that exposes the collection of named animation skeletal poses.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: Before exporting models with multiple skeletons to a USD file, merge all the skeletons into a single joint or bone hierarchy.

coverage.note: Blend shape weights are a component whose named weight sets can be read and written at runtime.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: BlendShapeWeightsComponent
sources.quote: A component that provides access to the current weights associated with all blend shape meshes on an entity.

coverage.note: A component performs GPU instancing over one entity's model, and instancing of mesh and texture data survives import from USD.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MeshInstancesComponent
sources.quote: A component that performs GPU instancing on the model of the same entity.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
sources.quote: RealityKit supports instancing of mesh and texture data from imported USD files.

coverage.note: This is the strongest interchange story in the subject. Composition is USD's: files reference other files and override what they reference, USDKit exposes layers and stages to Swift, and a USD stage can be rendered straight into an entity hierarchy.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: USD
sources.quote: USD files can reference other USD files, and even override the contents of referenced USD files, allowing a completely non-destructive workflow.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: USDKit
sources.quote: Because multiple layers can define or override the same primitive, the stage composes the contributions from each layer to produce the final scene.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: USDKit
sources.quote: A component that renders a USD stage as RealityKit entities.

coverage.note: One unit is one metre, and the physics simulation states the same unit independently.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
sources.quote: RealityKit uses Y-up orientation and meters as its unit scale.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsSimulationComponent
sources.quote: Each physics simulation component uses meters as its unit of distance

coverage.note: The platform has an avatar — the spatial Persona a person appears as in a shared session — but the app never sees it. The system places and renders Personas; there is no portable body description, no file, and no app-side representation to move anywhere else.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Adding spatial Persona support to an activity
sources.quote: A person who participates in SharePlay activities on Apple Vision Pro has the option to participate using their spatial Persona.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Adding spatial Persona support to an activity
sources.quote: The system arranges spatial Personas around the activity content, giving each person a clear view of the content and each other.

coverage.note: ARKit publishes one named joint hierarchy for tracked human bodies, with a stated neutral height, and a character has to be rigged to it to be driven. It is Apple's own list rather than an agreed interchange skeleton, and it exists for body tracking, not for carrying an avatar between worlds.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ARSkeletonDefinition
sources.quote: ARKit names particular joints that are crucial to body tracking.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ARSkeletonDefinition.defaultBody3D
sources.quote: The default height of this skeleton is 1.66 meters.

coverage.note: ARKit's named blend-shape coefficients for the face are the closest thing the industry has to a shared expression vocabulary, and many other systems copy the names. They are a tracking output on iOS front-camera sessions, not a format, and Apple defines no viseme set for speech.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ARFaceAnchor.BlendShapeLocation
sources.quote: ARKit provides many blend shape coefficients, resulting in a detailed model of a facial expression

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ARFaceAnchor
sources.quote: You can use blend shape coefficients to animate 2D or 3D content, such as a character or avatar, in ways that follow the user’s facial expressions.

coverage.note: A body-tracked entity plays a live person's motion on a virtual character, and a full-body inverse kinematics solver adapts a pose procedurally. Both require the character to be rigged to Apple's skeleton; there is no general mapping between two arbitrary rigs.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: BodyTrackedEntity
sources.quote: An entity used to animate a virtual character in an AR scene by tracking a real person.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: IKComponent
sources.quote: A component that allows you to procedurally animate a skeletal model using a full body inverse kinematics solver.

coverage.note: RealityKit documents a generic LevelOfDetailComponent (introduced in OS 27) that shows or hides child entities by camera distance, screen area or resolution metric. It is not avatar-specific: no reduced avatar representation, crowd rule or avatar profile is defined, and an exchange format for avatar detail levels is not described. sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: LevelOfDetailComponent (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: The component allows entities to automatically show/hide child entities based on viewing conditions, reducing rendering complexity for distant or small objects.

coverage.note: Nothing binds an avatar to a checkable identity; a spatial Persona belongs to the Apple account on the call and the app is given neither the Persona nor a credential about it. sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Adding spatial Persona support to an activity (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: Each person sees the facial expressions of other participants, what they’re looking at, and where they’re pointing.

coverage.note: A physics body component gives an entity mass and Newtonian response, and a separate motion component carries linear and angular velocity; a simulation component sets gravity and solver iterations for a subtree.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsBodyComponent
sources.quote: A component that defines an entity’s behavior in physics body simulations.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsMotionComponent
sources.quote: A component that controls the motion of the body in physics simulations.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsSimulationComponent
sources.quote: A component that controls localized physics simulations.

coverage.note: Collision shapes are a separate component from the visible mesh and also serve queries, ray casts and convex shape casts; box, convex mesh and triangle mesh shapes are named explicitly.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: CollisionComponent
sources.quote: This component holds the entity’s data related to participating in the scene’s physics simulation. It is also used to calculate collision queries, raycasts, and convex shape casts.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ShapeResource
sources.quote: A representation of a shape.

coverage.note: Joints link two entities at named pin poses with linear and angular limits, and live on a joints component inside a simulation.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsJoint
sources.quote: A type that describes physics joints.

coverage.note: A physics material resource carries static friction, dynamic friction and restitution.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: PhysicsMaterialResource
sources.quote: Material properties, like friction, of a physically simulated object.

coverage.note: Apple states no determinism guarantee for the simulation. The synchronised multi-device model is authority-and-replication over the network rather than a matching simulation on each device. Searched the symbol-title indexes of ARKit, RealityKit, USD, USDKit and GroupActivities (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/index/<framework>, current snapshot) and the pages named in the sources on 2026-10-19 for determinism, deterministic, fixed time step, reproducible; only a cloth time-step setting and a localized PhysicsSimulationComponent turned up; no page states that identical inputs give identical results on different devices.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: RealityKit (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: Animate objects, both manually and with physics simulations.

coverage.note: Cloth is documented: a RealityKit "Cloth simulation" collection (ClothSimulationComponent, ClothBodyComponent, collider, grab and force-volume components) introduced in OS 27 for iOS, iPadOS and visionOS. Missing: no volumetric soft body or other deformable solid is documented, and the collection is a RealityKit runtime API with no exchange format. Documentation availability is not a compilation, deployment, device-performance or interchange test. Searched the symbol-title indexes of ARKit, RealityKit, USD, USDKit and GroupActivities (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/index/<framework>) on 2026-10-19 for cloth, soft body, deform; found the cloth family and BlendShapeDeformer (animation).

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Cloth simulation (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: Add fabric, soft surfaces, and draping materials that bend, fold, and respond to forces and contact in your 3D scenes.

coverage.note: A trigger volume is an invisible shape that reports entry and exit without taking part in the simulation, and any collision entity can be switched into trigger mode.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: TriggerVolume
sources.quote: An invisible 3D shape that detects when objects enter or exit a given region of space.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: CollisionComponent
sources.quote: A trigger entity doesn’t have any impact on the rigid bodies in the scene, but can trigger code or Reality Composer behaviors when a rigid body entity overlaps it.

coverage.note: Sound is played from an entity and follows it; playback is spatial unless the app asks otherwise, and mix groups gather several playing sounds under one gain.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SpatialAudioComponent
sources.quote: The audio system continuously updates the position and orientation of spatial audio sources automatically, so sounds come from an entity wherever it goes and wherever it points.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: AudioMixGroup
sources.quote: A group that manages the playback properties of multiple playing sounds.

coverage.note: Three rendering modes ship: spatial with distance attenuation and directivity, ambient projected from an angle without reverberation, and channel routed straight to the outputs. Spatial sources are mono only, so a multichannel asset is mixed down before spatialization.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SpatialAudioComponent
sources.quote: Spatial audio sources emit only a single channel (that is, mono). The engine mixes any stereo or multichannel audio resources down to a single channel before spatialization.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: AmbientAudioComponent
sources.quote: Ambient audio sources emit each channel of an audio resource from an angle projected from the entity, without reverberation.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ChannelAudioComponent
sources.quote: Channel audio sources route the audio resource’s channels directly to the device’s output without any spatialization or reverberation applied.

coverage.note: On visionOS the real room is simulated by default and colours every spatial source; a reverb component overrides it with a named preset for an authored environment.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: ReverbComponent
sources.quote: In visionOS, an acoustic simulation of a person’s real environment reverberates the spatial audio sources by default.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SpatialAudioComponent
sources.quote: Spatial audio sources incorporate a person’s environment acoustics so that they blend in naturally with the surrounding area.

coverage.note: Surfaces have acoustic materials with per-band absorption and scattering, which is the input an occlusion model needs, and a named preset list covers common real surfaces. What is missing is the control: no documented obstruction or occlusion setting, and no way to ask whether geometry blocks a given source.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Audio.Material
sources.quote: An audio material defines how a surface absorbs and scatters sound energy across frequency bands.

coverage.note: An audio resource loads from a file or a URL and its loading strategy decides how the data is handled before and during playback, which covers reading a long asset without holding it in memory. There is no network audio delivery of the subject's own.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: AudioFileResource
sources.quote: An audio resource that you load from a file or from a URL.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: AudioFileResource
sources.quote: A container for different strategies on how to handle resources’ data before and during playback.

coverage.note: Neither framework carries live voice. A shared session on this platform runs on a FaceTime call, and the call carries the talking; the app gets synchronised activity data, not an audio channel it can route into the scene.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Group Activities
sources.quote: This framework leverages the FaceTime infrastructure to synchronize your app’s activities and to invite other participants to join those activities.

coverage.note: Every entity has a synchronization component with a network identifier, and the multipeer service keeps the scenes of connected devices matching automatically. It is same-app replication: both ends run the same build of the same app.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SynchronizationComponent
sources.quote: A component that synchronizes an entity between processes and networked applications.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MultipeerConnectivityService
sources.quote: RealityKit uses this class to automatically sync scenes with other connected devices running the same app.

coverage.note: One process owns an entity, the owner can be read, ownership can be handed to a named peer, and a transfer mode governs whether a request is granted.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: SynchronizationComponent
sources.quote: A Boolean that indicates whether the calling process owns the entity.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MultipeerConnectivityService
sources.quote: Transfers ownership of the given entity to the named network device.

coverage.note: Nothing decides what each peer needs; the multipeer session synchronises the scene to all connected devices. Searched the symbol-title indexes of ARKit, RealityKit, USD, USDKit and GroupActivities (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/index/<framework>, current snapshot) and the pages named in the sources on 2026-10-19 for interest, relevance, area of interest, filter; only collision and navigation filters; no setting limits what each peer receives from scene synchronization.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MultipeerConnectivityService (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: A service that provides scene synchronization among all peers in a multipeer connectivity session.

coverage.note: No prediction and no reconciliation of synchronised state is offered. Searched the symbol-title indexes of ARKit, RealityKit, USD, USDKit and GroupActivities (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/index/<framework>, current snapshot) and the pages named in the sources on 2026-10-19 for prediction, reconcile, rollback, interpolation, latency; predictAnchor and the predicted tracking mode concern sensor tracking, not network state; no network prediction or correction API.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MultipeerConnectivityService (DocC Markdown)
sources.quote: A service that provides scene synchronization among all peers in a multipeer connectivity session.

coverage.note: The one transport the subject ships is peer-to-peer: RealityKit's synchronization service is built on Multipeer Connectivity, which runs over infrastructure Wi-Fi, peer-to-peer Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. There is no client-server transport and no internet-scale session.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: MultipeerConnectivityService
sources.quote: A service that provides scene synchronization among all peers in a multipeer connectivity session.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Multipeer Connectivity
sources.quote: In iOS, the framework uses infrastructure Wi-Fi networks, peer-to-peer Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth personal area networks for the underlying transport.

coverage.note: Live video reaches the scene, but the transport is not the subject's. A video component takes a player the app supplies and draws its output in three dimensions; nothing in ARKit or RealityKit moves an audio or video stream between participants.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: VideoPlayerComponent
sources.quote: A component that supports general video-playback experience with an AV player.

coverage.note: Joining is done by two other frameworks. Nearby devices invite each other through Multipeer Connectivity, and a shared session across a call is a SharePlay group activity on the FaceTime infrastructure. RealityKit adds only a compatibility check so a host can refuse a peer on an incompatible version.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Group Activities
sources.quote: This framework leverages the FaceTime infrastructure to synchronize your app’s activities and to invite other participants to join those activities.

coverage.note: There is no leaving one world and arriving in another with state intact. RealityKit's portal looks into a second world inside the same app's scene, and entities may cross its boundary, but both worlds belong to one process; nothing crosses to another publisher's experience.
